 Social Security Is Giving Retirees a Raise in 2027 But One Old Rule Will Quietly Tax More of Them
 A Social Security card, coins, dollar bills, and a calculator are arranged on an American flag. (Credit: Image via Shutterstock) Jeannine Mancini Sat, November 7, 2026 at 11:30 PM EST 7 min read Benzinga and Yahoo Finance LLC may earn commission or revenue on some items through the links below. 
 A bigger Social Security check sounds like good news. But for millions of retirees, there's a catch hiding in the tax code — one that hasn't budged in more than three decades. 
 The Social Security Administration announced a 3.6% cost-of-living adjustment for 2027, giving the average retired worker an estimated $75 more per month. That lifts the average monthly benefit from $2,095 to $2,170, or roughly $900 more over a full year. 
 Nearly 72 million Social Security beneficiaries will receive the increase beginning in January. About 7.3 million Supplemental Security Income recipients will see higher payments starting Dec. 31. The adjustment covers roughly 76 million Americans, according to the SSA.

 But while benefits are getting a boost, one set of numbers remains frozen. The income thresholds that determine whether Social Security benefits are subject to federal income tax haven't changed since 1994. 
 A Bigger Check, But the Same Old Tax Thresholds 
 The 2027 adjustment brings several other changes. The maximum amount of annual earnings subject to Social Security payroll taxes will rise from $184,500 to $192,300. The maximum monthly benefit for someone retiring at full retirement age will increase from $4,152 to $4,188. 
 SSI's federal payment standard will also climb to $1,029 per month for an individual and $1,544 for an eligible couple. 
 Yet the income limits governing taxes on Social Security benefits remain exactly where they were decades ago. 
 The calculation starts with what's known as combined income, or provisional income. It includes adjusted gross income, tax-exempt interest and half of a person's annual Social Security benefits. 
 For federal income tax purposes, the thresholds are: 
 Single filers: Benefits generally aren't taxable when combined income is $25,000 or less. Above $25,000, up to 50% of benefits can be included in taxable income. Above $34,000, as much as 85% can be included. 
 Married couples filing jointly: The corresponding thresholds are $32,000 and $44,000.

 These limits originated with legislation passed in 1983 and 1993, with the higher tier taking effect in 1994. They were never indexed for inflation or wage growth. 
 Story Continues That creates an increasingly tight squeeze. Social Security checks rise with inflation, but the income limits used to determine whether those benefits are taxable stay put. 
 More Social Security Money, More Taxable Income 
 Consider the average retired worker receiving an additional $75 per month. That's approximately $900 in added benefits over the year. 
 Because half of Social Security benefits count toward combined income, that increase adds roughly $450 to the income calculation. 
 For someone already approaching one of the frozen thresholds, even a relatively modest increase could push combined income higher and cause a larger portion of benefits to become taxable. 
 Under the rules, up to 50% of benefits can be taxable once combined income exceeds $25,000 for single filers or $32,000 for married couples filing jointly. Once income passes $34,000 for single filers or $44,000 for joint filers, up to 85% of benefits can be included in taxable income.

 That doesn't mean retirees pay an 85% tax rate. It means that portion of their Social Security benefits can be subject to their regular federal income tax rate. 
 The Congressional Budget Office estimates that slightly more than half of Social Security beneficiaries will owe federal income taxes on their benefits in 2026. Its August report also explains that the fixed thresholds allow a growing share of benefits to become subject to taxation as incomes and benefit payments rise. 
 There is also a temporary tax break worth knowing about. Eligible taxpayers age 65 and older can claim an additional $6,000 deduction for tax years 2025 through 2028. The deduction can reduce taxable income, although it doesn't change the underlying Social Security taxation thresholds. 
 The 2027 COLA will put more money in retirees' monthly checks. But with the tax thresholds still stuck in 1994, the full increase won't necessarily translate into more money kept after taxes. 
 The SSA says individual COLA notices will become available through personal my Social Security accounts in late November. Notices will also arrive by mail in December.

 Building Wealth Across More Than Just the Market 
 Building a resilient portfolio means thinking beyond a single asset or market trend. Economic cycles shift, sectors rise and fall, and no one investment performs well in every environment. That's why many investors look to diversify with platforms that provide access to real estate, fixed-income opportunities, precious metals, and even self-directed retirement accounts. By spreading exposure across multiple asset classes, it becomes easier to manage risk, capture steady returns, and create long-term wealth that isn't tied to the fortunes of just one company or industry. 
 EquityMultiple 
 For accredited investors looking beyond stocks and bonds, EquityMultiple provides access to vetted commercial real estate deals starting at $5,000 , with only ~5% of opportunities passing their due diligence process. 
 Arrived 
 Backed by Jeff Bezos, Arrived Homes makes real estate investing accessible with a low barrier to entry. Investors can buy fractional shares of single-family rentals and vacation homes starting with as little as $100 . This allows everyday investors to diversify into real estate, collect rental income, and build long-term wealth without needing to manage properties directly. 
 American PowerGen 
 As artificial intelligence drives a surge in electricity demand, reliable power generation is becoming a critical part of the technology ecosystem. American PowerGen is developing natural gas-fired power plants in Texas, a fast-growing market fueled by AI data centers, manufacturing expansion, and population growth. By advancing projects through permitting, fuel supply, and grid interconnection, the company is positioning itself to help meet rising energy needs while offering investors exposure to the infrastructure supporting the next wave of AI and industrial growth. 
 Bito 
 As AI coding tools take on more of the work traditionally done by developers, companies are facing new challenges around code quality, context and the rising cost of AI-powered development. Bito is building software designed to help AI coding agents better understand complex codebases while helping companies control AI development costs. Founded by former PubMatic executives, Bito has raised more than $10 million from institutional and individual investors and is now raising additional capital through a Wefunder offering, giving investors an opportunity to invest in a company targeting an emerging need within the rapidly expanding AI software market. 
 FarmTogether 
 Farmland has historically held its value through market volatility and delivered returns uncorrelated to stocks and bonds. For accredited investors, FarmTogether offers direct access to high-quality U.S. farmland starting at $15,000 — fully managed, with no landlord headaches. 
 Fundrise 
 Private real estate and private credit can add income and stability to a stock-heavy portfolio. Fundrise offers access to diversified private real estate and credit strategies through an easy-to-use platform, with professionally managed portfolios designed to generate passive income and long-term growth.
